title: The Lord's Prayer as the new form of prayer and summary of the gospel
english: The Spirit of God, the Word of God, and the Reason of God—the Word of Reason, the Reason of the Word, and the Spirit of both—Jesus Christ our Lord, determined a new form of prayer for the new disciples of the new covenant. For in this matter too it was fitting that new wine be stored in new wineskins and a new patch be sewn onto a new garment (Matthew 9:17). Whatever had existed before was either changed, like circumcision, or completed, like the rest of the law, or fulfilled, like prophecy, or perfected, like faith itself. The new grace of God renewed all things from carnal to spiritual by introducing the gospel, the canceller of all oldness that was before. In this gospel our Lord Jesus Christ was approved as the Spirit of God, the Word of God, and the Reason of God: the Spirit by which he had power, the Word by which he taught, the Reason by which he came.

So then, the prayer established by Christ is established from three things: from the word by which it is spoken, from the Spirit by which alone it has power, and from the reason by which it is taught. John had also taught his disciples to pray, but all the things of John were being built up beforehand for Christ, until Christ was increased—John himself foretold that Christ must increase and John must decrease (John 3:30)—and the whole work of the forerunner passed over with his spirit to the Lord. Therefore it is not recorded in what words John taught people to pray, because earthly things yielded to heavenly things. John says, "He who is from the earth speaks earthly things, and he who comes from heaven speaks what he has seen" (John 3:31). And what belonging to the Lord Christ is not heavenly, as this teaching on prayer also is?

Let us consider, then, blessed ones, his heavenly wisdom. First, concerning the command to pray in secret, by which he both demanded the faith of a person—so that one would trust that the sight and hearing of almighty God are present even under roofs and in a hidden place—and desired the modesty of faith, so that the one whom a person trusts to hear and see everywhere would receive that person's worship for himself alone. The wisdom that follows in the next command likewise pertains to faith and the modesty of faith, if we do not think we must approach the Lord with a flood of words, since we are certain that he looks upon us of his own accord. And yet this brevity, which makes for the third step of wisdom, is supported by the substance of a great and blessed interpretation, and as much as it is compressed in words, so much it is expanded in meanings. For it has not only embraced the proper duties of prayer—the worship of God or the petition of a person—but nearly every word of the Lord and every remembrance of his teaching, so that truly in this prayer a summary of the whole gospel is contained.
orientation: Tertullian opens his treatise by presenting the Lord's Prayer as the new form of prayer Christ gave to his new disciples, replacing and fulfilling all that came before.

title: The Father in heaven: faith, sonship, and the church as mother
english: It begins with God's own testimony and the merit of faith when we say, "Father who art in heaven." For we both pray to God and commend faith, whose merit is this very address. It is written: "To those who believed in him he gave the power to be called children of God" (John 1:12). Yet the Lord very often declared God to be our Father, and indeed commanded that we call no one on earth father, except the one we have in heaven (Matthew 23:9). So when we pray in this way, we are also carrying out a command. Happy are those who acknowledge the Father.

This is what Israel is reproached for, what the Spirit testifies to heaven and earth: "I begot children," he says, "and they did not know me" (Isaiah 1:2). And when we say Father, we also name God. This address is both of piety and of power. In the Father, the Son is also invoked. "For I and the Father are one," he says (John 10:30). Not even mother church is passed over. For in the Son and the Father the mother is recognized, from whom the name of both Father and Son is established. So with one word or name we honor God together with his own, remember the command, and mark those who have forgotten the Father.
orientation: Tertullian has just said the Lord's Prayer is a summary of the whole gospel, and now he begins expounding its first words, 'Our Father who art in heaven.'

title: The Father's name revealed in the Son and hallowed in us
english: The name of God the Father had been disclosed to no one. Even Moses, who had asked about him, heard a different name. To us it has been revealed in the Son. For who indeed is the Son? He is a new name for the Father. "I have come," he says, "in my Father's name" (John 5:43), and again, "Father, glorify your name" (John 12:28), and more plainly, "I have made your name known to men" (John 17:6). So we ask that it be hallowed. Not that it is fitting for human beings to wish God well, as if there were someone else from whom good could be wished for him, or as if he would suffer unless we wished it. Certainly it is fitting for God to be blessed by every person in every place and time, because we always owe him the remembrance of his benefits. But this petition also serves in place of blessing. After all, when is the name of God not holy and hallowed through itself, since it hallows all others from itself? The surrounding company of angels never ceases to say, "Holy, holy, holy" (Isaiah 6:3). Therefore we too, if we have deserved it, are white-robed candidates of the angels, and from this very moment we learn that heavenly voice addressed to God and the office of future glory. So much for the glory of God. As for our own petition, when we say, "Hallowed be your name," we ask that it be hallowed in us, who are in him, and at the same time in others whom the grace of God still awaits, so that we may also obey this command by praying for everyone, even for our enemies. That is why, with the utterance left suspended, we do not say, "Hallowed be it in us," but we say it for all.
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the first petition of the Lord's Prayer, 'Hallowed be your name,' after having explained the address 'Father.'

title: God's will in heaven and on earth
english: Following this pattern we add: “Your will be done in heaven and on earth.” We do not say this because someone is resisting so that God’s will cannot be done, and we pray for the success of his will. Rather, we ask that his will be done in all things. For in the figurative interpretation of flesh and spirit, we ourselves are heaven and earth. Yet even if it must be understood simply, the sense of the petition is still the same: that God’s will be done in us on earth, so that it may also be done in heaven. What does God will except that we walk according to his teaching? We ask, then, that he supply us with the substance and power of his will, so that we may be saved both in heaven and on earth, because the highest point of his will is the salvation of those whom he has adopted.

There is also that will of God which the Lord carried out by preaching, by working, and by enduring. For if he himself declared that he did not his own will but the Father’s, then without doubt the things he was doing were the Father’s will. To these things we are now summoned as to examples, so that we too may preach and work and endure even to death. To be able to fulfill these things, we need the will of God. Likewise, when we say, “Your will be done,” we are wishing ourselves well in this too: that there is nothing evil in God’s will, even if something is inflicted on each person otherwise according to their deserts. By this saying we also warn ourselves beforehand toward endurance. The Lord too, when under the pressure of his passion he wished to show the weakness of the flesh already in his own flesh, said, “Father, remove this cup,” and then remembered, “Yet not my will, but that your will be done.” He himself was the will and power of the Father, and yet he handed himself over to the Father’s will to demonstrate the endurance that is owed.
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the third petition of the Lord's Prayer, after having treated the hallowing of God's name.

title: The Coming of the Kingdom
english: The petition “Your kingdom come” also points to the same thing as “Your will be done”: namely, in us. For when does God not reign, when the heart of every king is in his hand? But whatever we wish for ourselves, we direct toward him, and we credit to him what we expect from him. So if the manifestation of the Lord’s kingdom belongs to God’s will and to our expectation, why do some people, by a certain lingering in the world, demand it, since the kingdom of God, which we pray may come, tends toward the consummation of the age? We desire to reign sooner, not to serve longer. Even if it had not been prescribed beforehand in the prayer that we should ask for the coming of the kingdom, we would have uttered that cry of our own accord, hastening toward the embrace of our hope. The souls of the martyrs under the altar cry out to the Lord in envy: “How long will you not avenge our blood on the inhabitants of the earth, Lord?” (Revelation 6:10). For their vengeance is certainly directed from the end of the age. Indeed, how quickly may your kingdom come, Lord: the desire of Christians, the confusion of nations, the exultation of angels, for which we struggle, or rather for which we pray.
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the petition 'Thy kingdom come' from the Lord's Prayer, arguing that it looks toward the end of the age.

title: Daily bread as Christ and the Father's provision
english: But how elegantly divine wisdom arranged the order of prayer! After heavenly things, that is, after God's name, God's will, and God's kingdom, it also made room for earthly necessities in our petition. For the Lord had commanded: "Seek first the kingdom, and then these things will also be added to you" (Matthew 6:33). Nevertheless, we should understand "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11) spiritually rather than carnally. For Christ is our bread, because Christ is life, and life is bread. "I am," he says, "the bread of life" (John 6:35), and a little before that: "The bread is the word of the living God, who comes down from heaven" (John 6:33). Then too his body is reckoned in the bread: "This is my body" (Matthew 26:26). Therefore, by asking for daily bread, we ask for permanence in Christ and indivisibility from his body. But because this phrase is also admitted carnally, it cannot happen without the reverence of spiritual teaching. For he commands that bread be asked for, which alone is necessary for the faithful; the nations seek after everything else. So he drives this home with examples and handles it again in parables, when he says: "Does a father take bread from his children and hand it to dogs?" (Matthew 15:26). Likewise: "Does he hand a stone to his son who asks for bread?" (Matthew 7:9). For he shows what children should expect from a father. But that night-time knocker also asked for bread (Luke 11:5). And rightly he added: "Give us today," since he had already commanded: "Do not think about tomorrow, what you will eat" (Matthew 6:34). To this matter he also fitted the parable of that man who, when his crops came in, thought about enlarging his barns and the spaces of long security, and he dies that very night (Luke 12:16-20).
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the fourth petition of the Lord's Prayer, the request for daily bread, after having treated the petitions for God's name, will, and kingdom.

title: Forgiveness as confession and the parable of the unforgiving servant
english: It followed that, having observed God's generosity, we should also pray for his mercy. For what good will food do us if we are actually reckoned before him like a bull for sacrifice? The Lord knew that he alone was without sin. So he teaches us to ask: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). Confession is the asking of pardon, because whoever asks for pardon confesses sin. In this way repentance is shown to be acceptable to God, since he desires it rather than the death of a sinner.

In the Scriptures, debt is a figure for sin, because it is likewise owed to judgment and exacted from a person, and it does not escape the justice of exaction unless the exaction is forgiven—just as the master forgave that servant his debt (Matthew 18:27). The whole parable points to this. For the same servant, after being set free by his master, does not likewise spare his own debtor, and for that reason he is denounced before his master and handed over to the torturer to pay the last farthing, that is, every sin down to the smallest (Matthew 18:34). This applies to us because we also declare that we forgive our debtors.

And elsewhere, from this same form of prayer, he says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). And when Peter asked whether he should forgive a brother seven times, he said: “No, seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:22). He did this to reform the law for the better, since in Genesis vengeance was reckoned sevenfold for Cain, but seventy-sevenfold for Lamech (Genesis 4:24).
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the fifth petition of the Lord's Prayer, 'Forgive us our debts,' after having treated the petition for daily bread.

title: The final petition: deliverance from temptation and evil
english: To the fullness of this concise prayer he added that we should ask not only for sins to be forgiven, but for them to be turned away entirely: “Lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6:13). That is, do not allow us to be led in—by him, of course, who tempts. Far be it from the Lord to seem to tempt anyone, as if he did not know each person's faith or was eager to cast them down. Weakness and malice belong to the devil. For Abraham too was ordered to sacrifice his son not for the sake of tempting his faith, but of testing it, so that through him God might make an example of his own command, which he was soon going to give: that no one should hold pledges dearer than God. When the Lord himself was tempted by the devil, he showed who is the overseer and craftsman of temptation. He confirms this point later when he says: “Pray, so that you may not be tempted” (Matthew 26:41). And they were tempted by deserting the Lord, because they had given themselves to sleep rather than prayer. So the closing petition answers and interprets what “lead us not into temptation” means. For this is what it means: “But deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13).
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the last petition of the Lord's Prayer, after discussing the forgiveness of debts.

title: The Lord's Prayer as a compendium of all duty
english: In the compass of a very few words, how many sayings of the prophets, the gospels, the apostles are touched upon—the Lord's own discourses, parables, examples, commands! How many duties are discharged at once! The honor of God in the Father, the testimony of faith in the name, the offering of obedience in the will, the remembrance of hope in the kingdom, the petition for life in the bread, the confession of debts in the plea for pardon, the anxiety of temptations in the request for protection. What wonder is there in this? God alone could teach how he wished to be prayed to. Therefore the religion of prayer was established by him, and from his Spirit—already at that moment when it was being carried forth from the divine mouth—it was given life, and by its own privilege it ascends into heaven, commending to the Father what the Son taught.
orientation: Tertullian has just begun his treatise by praising the Lord's Prayer as a summary of the whole gospel, and now he enumerates the duties it covers in each petition.

title: Petitions beyond the Lord's Prayer
english: Yet since the Lord looks after human needs, he said separately, after handing over the teaching of praying, “Ask, and you will receive” (Matthew 7:7). There are things to be asked for according to each person's circumstances. Once the lawful and ordinary prayer has been placed first as a foundation, those who approach have the right to build their own petitions of desires upon it from outside—provided they still remember the precepts.
orientation: Tertullian is explaining how Christians may add their own particular requests to the fixed and ordinary prayer that Christ taught.

title: Peace with brothers before approaching God
english: So that we may not be as far from God's ears as we are from the precepts, the memory of the precepts paves a way for prayers to heaven. The chief of them is this: we must not go up to God's altar before we have resolved any discord or offense we have contracted with our brothers. For what kind of thing is it to approach the peace of God without peace? To approach the remission of debts with retention? How will a man placate the Father while he is angry at his brother, when all anger has been forbidden to us from the beginning? For Joseph, sending his brothers away to bring back their father, said, "Do not be angry on the way" (Genesis 45:24). He was certainly warning us—for our teaching is called by another name, the Way—not to walk toward the Father in anger while we are set on the way of prayer. From that point on the Lord, amplifying the law, places anger against a brother above homicide. He does not permit it to be discharged even by an evil word. Even if one must be angry, it is not to go beyond the setting of the sun, as the apostle admonishes (Ephesians 4:26). How reckless it is either to pass a day without prayer while you delay satisfying your brother, or to lose your prayer by persisting in anger!
orientation: Tertullian is explaining the first and chief precept of prayer: before going up to God's altar, a Christian must resolve any discord or offense with fellow believers.

title: Prayer requires a spirit matching the Holy Spirit
english: The intention of prayer must be free not only from anger but from every disturbance of the mind whatsoever. It must be sent out from a spirit of the same kind as the Spirit to whom it is sent. A polluted spirit cannot be recognized by the Holy Spirit, nor a sad one by the joyful, nor a hindered one by the free. No one receives an adversary; no one admits anyone except his equal.
orientation: Tertullian is continuing his argument that prayer must be offered from a pure and peaceful heart, now extending the requirement from freedom from anger to freedom from every disturbance of the mind.

title: True cleanness of hands is spiritual, not ritual washing
english: But what sense does it make to go to prayer with hands washed while the spirit is dirty, when the hands themselves need spiritual cleanness so that they may be lifted up pure from falsehood, murder, cruelty, poisoning, idolatry, and the other stains that are conceived in the spirit and carried out by the work of the hands? These are the true cleannesses, not the ones most people superstitiously fuss over by taking water before every prayer, even when they come from a bath of the whole body. When I investigated this rather carefully and asked for the reason, I found that it is a commemoration of Pilate washing his hands in the handing over of the Lord (Matthew 27:24). We worship the Lord; we do not hand him over. In fact, we ought to oppose the example of the betrayer and not wash our hands for that reason. Unless we wash them because of some defilement of human conduct for the sake of conscience, our hands are clean enough, since we washed them once for all with the whole body in Christ.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the purity required for prayer is inward, not the superstitious washing of hands that some practice even after a full bath.

title: Israel's unclean hands versus Christian hands spread in confession of Christ
english: Israel may wash every limb every day, yet it is never clean. Its hands are certainly always unclean, encrusted forever with the blood of the prophets and of the Lord himself. For that reason, as hereditary guilty ones by the conscience of their fathers, they do not dare even to lift their hands to the Lord, lest some Isaiah cry out, lest Christ shudder. But we not only lift our hands—we spread them out—and as we sing of the Lord's passion and pray, we confess to Christ.
orientation: Tertullian is contrasting the perpetual uncleanness of Israel's hands, stained by the blood of the prophets and the Lord, with the Christian practice of lifting and spreading the hands in prayer.

title: Rejecting customs without divine authority
english: But since I have touched on one empty observance, I will not hesitate to point out the rest as well. They rightly deserve to be reproached as vanity, since they are done without the authority of any command from the Lord or the apostles. Practices of this kind are counted not to religion but to superstition. They are affected and forced, and they belong to a curious rather than a rational office. Certainly they should be restrained for this reason at least: that they make themselves equal to the gentiles. An example is the practice of some who pray with their cloaks laid aside. That is how the nations approach their idols. If this were really necessary, the apostles, who teach about the proper dress for prayer, would have included it. Unless someone thinks Paul left his cloak with Carpus during prayer. God, of course, does not hear people in cloaks. The same God heard three holy men praying in the furnace of the Babylonian king with their trousers and their turbans on (Daniel 3:21).
orientation: Tertullian is criticizing practices of prayer that have no dominical or apostolic authority, and he now gives the example of praying with cloaks laid aside.

title: Sitting after prayer is not a rule
english: I do not see the reason why some people have a custom of sitting down after the appointed prayer, except that they are following a childish whim. What if that Hermas, whose book is usually called “The Shepherd,” had not sat down on his bed after finishing prayer but had done something else? Would we claim that too as a rule? Certainly not. For even now it is stated simply, “When I had prayed and sat down on my bed,” for the order of the narrative, not as a pattern of teaching. Otherwise there will be no place to pray except where there is a bed. In fact, anyone who sits on a chair or a bench would be acting against Scripture.

Furthermore, since the nations do the same thing by sitting down after their little images have been worshipped, it deserves to be condemned in us for this reason too: that it is practiced before idols. To this is added the charge of irreverence, which even the nations themselves should understand, if they had any sense. For it is irreverent to sit down under the gaze and directly in the sight of someone whom you are at that very moment revering and venerating. How much more irreligious is it to do this under the gaze of the living God, with the angel of prayer still standing by? Unless we are reproaching God that prayer has wearied us.
orientation: Tertullian is criticizing customs added to prayer, and here he rejects the practice of sitting down after finishing prayer as if it were required.

title: Modesty in posture and voice
english: But when we pray with modesty and humility, we will commend our prayers to God all the more. We should not even lift our hands too high, but lift them temperately and properly, and we should not raise our face into boldness. For that tax collector who prayed humbled and cast down, not only in his prayer but in his face, departed more justified than the most shameless Pharisee (Luke 18:14).

The sounds of the voice also ought to be subdued. How much windpipe do we need if we are heard because of our volume? God is not a hearer of the voice but of the heart, just as he is an observer of the heart. The demon of the Pythian oracle, the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, says, "I understand the mute, and I hear the one who does not speak." Do God's ears wait for sound? How then could Jonah's prayer escape from the deepest belly of the sea monster, through the entrails of so great a beast, from the very abysses, through so great a mass of water, all the way to heaven (Jonah 2:1-2)?
What more do those who pray more loudly accomplish, except that they make a din for their neighbors? Indeed, by broadcasting their requests, what less do they do than if they were praying in public?
orientation: Tertullian is giving practical rules for how Christians should pray, and has just begun discussing the modest bearing of the body.

title: The kiss of peace on fast days
english: Another custom has now taken hold. Those who are fasting, after praying with the brothers, withhold the kiss of peace, which is the seal of prayer. When should peace be shared with the brothers more than when the prayer of the one working rises more commendably, so that they may share in our work, refreshed by the peace they made with a brother? What prayer is complete when separated from the kiss of peace? Whom does peace hinder while he serves the Lord? What kind of sacrifice is it from which people depart without peace? Whatever the prayer may be, it will not be better than observing the precept by which we are commanded to hide our fasting. For now we are recognized as fasting by abstaining from the kiss. But even if there is some reason, do not be guilty against this precept: you can, if necessary, postpone the peace at home, among those from whom your fasting cannot be entirely hidden. But wherever else you can hide your work, you should remember the precept. In this way you will satisfy the teaching in public and the custom at home. So also on the day of Easter, when fasting is a common and as it were public religious observance, we rightly set aside the kiss, not caring about hiding what we do together with everyone.
orientation: Tertullian is discussing the customs of prayer and now addresses the practice of withholding the kiss of peace on fast days.

title: Fasting days and the Eucharist do not cancel each other
english: In the same way, many people think that on fast days they should not take part in the prayers of the sacrifices, because the fast day must be ended when the body of the Lord has been received. Does the Eucharist, then, undo a service devoted to God, or does it bind us more closely to God? Will your fast day not be more solemn if you also stand at the altar of God? When the body of the Lord has been received and reserved, both things are preserved: participation in the sacrifice and performance of the duty. If the fast day takes its name from a military example, for we are also God's army, then surely no joy or sorrow that comes upon the camp breaks up the soldiers' watches. For joy will carry out the teaching more willingly, and sorrow more carefully.
orientation: Tertullian is addressing customs of prayer and worship, now arguing that receiving the Lord's body on a fast day does not dissolve the fast-day observance.

title: The Variety of Observance About Women's Dress
english: But as for the dress of women, differences in practice have led us, people of no standing at all, to reconsider the matter after the most holy apostle. We do so shamelessly, except that it is not shameless if we reconsider it according to the apostle. On the modesty of attire and adornment there is indeed an open prescription, even from Peter. With the same mouth, because with the same Spirit as Paul, he restrains the glory of clothing, the pride of gold, and the seductive elaborateness of hair.
orientation: Tertullian is beginning his discussion of the customs of prayer, and here he turns to the question of women's dress and adornment, saying that after the apostle Paul's teaching it is shameful for Christians to reopen the matter.

title: Should virgins be veiled? The opponents' argument from Paul's wording
english: But since the churches observe this practice without distinction, as if the matter were uncertain, it must be reconsidered: should virgins be veiled or not? Those who allow virgins to go with uncovered heads seem to rely on this argument: the apostle did not name virgins specifically when he said women should be veiled. They argue that he did not name the sex itself by saying females, but a degree of the sex by saying women. For if he had named the sex, saying females, he would have made an absolute ruling about every woman. But when he names one degree of the sex, he separates another by remaining silent. He could have, they say, either named virgins specifically or, by way of summary, females generally.
orientation: Tertullian is opening the debate over whether virgins must be veiled, and here he states the argument of those who allow virgins to go with uncovered heads.

title: The word 'woman' includes virgins
english: Those who grant this exemption should think carefully about the meaning of the word itself. What is a woman, from the very first pages of the sacred writings? They will find that it is a name of the sex, not a degree of the sex. For God called Eve a woman and a female before she had known a man: female as the general name of the sex, woman as a particular name of the sex. So since Eve was still unmarried when she received the name woman, that word became common to the virgin as well. No wonder, then, that the apostle, moved by the same Spirit who composed all divine Scripture and that passage in Genesis, used the same word when he said woman, a word that fits the virgin too through the example of unmarried Eve.

Everything else agrees with this. By not naming virgins, as he does elsewhere when he teaches about marrying, he makes clear enough that he is speaking of every woman and the whole sex, and that no distinction is made between a woman and a virgin, whom he does not name at all. For when he remembers to distinguish elsewhere, where the difference requires it—and he distinguishes both kinds by naming each with its own word—when he does not distinguish and does not name either one, he wants no difference to be understood.

What about this? In the Greek language in which the apostle wrote, it is customary to say women rather than females—that is, gynaikas rather than theleias. So if this word is regularly used as the name of the sex, standing in for female, then he named the sex when he said gynaika. And the virgin is included in the sex.

The statement is also perfectly clear. Every woman, Paul says, who prays or prophesies with uncovered head dishonors her head (1 Corinthians 11:5). What is every woman but every age, every rank, every condition? By saying every he excludes no woman, just as he excludes no man and no veiling; for he likewise says every man (1 Corinthians 11:4). So just as in the male sex the unbearded youth is forbidden to veil under the name man, in the female sex the virgin is commanded to veil under the name woman. Let the younger age follow the teaching of the older equally in both sexes. Or let male virgins be veiled too, if female virgins are not veiled, since they too are not named explicitly. A man and an unbearded youth would be different things, if a woman and a virgin are different things.

He says, of course, that veiling is necessary because of the angels, since the angels fell away from God because of the daughters of men (Genesis 6:1–4). Who would argue that only women—that is, those already married and dead to virginity—are objects of desire? Unless virgins are not allowed to excel in beauty and find lovers? Let us rather consider whether they desired virgins alone, since Scripture says daughters of men, when it could have said wives of men or females without distinction. And when it says they took them as wives (Genesis 6:2), it points to this: those who are taken as wives are those who are free to marry. It would have spoken differently about those who were not free. So they are free both through widowhood and through virginity. Thus by naming the sex generally as daughters, he mixed the kinds within the genus.

Likewise when he says that nature itself teaches that females should be veiled, since it has assigned hair as a covering to women (1 Corinthians 11:14–15), has not the same covering and the same honor of the head been assigned to virgins too? If it is shameful for a woman to be shaved, it is equally so for a virgin (1 Corinthians 11:6). For those in whom one condition of the head is appointed, one teaching for the head is required—even for those virgins whom childhood protects. For from the beginning she was named female.

This is what Israel also observes. But if it did not observe it, our law, enlarged and completed, would claim the addition for itself. Let it be excused for placing the veil on virgins too. For now, let the age that does not know its own sex keep the privilege of simplicity. For Eve and Adam, when it happened that they knew, immediately covered what they had recognized (Genesis 3:7). Certainly in those whose childhood has changed, age ought to be generous to teaching just as it is to nature. For they are marked out for the members and duties of women. No one is a virgin from the time she can marry, since her age has already married her to its own husband—that is, to time.

But someone has vowed herself to God. Even so, from that point she changes her hair and turns her whole appearance to that of a woman. Let her then assert the whole thing and present herself entirely as a virgin: what she hides for God's sake, let her fully veil. It matters to us that God's grace be exercised, that we entrust it to the knowledge of God alone, so that we do not receive from men what we hope for from God. Why do you uncover before God what you cover before men? Will you be more modest in public than in the church? If it is God's grace and you have received it, why do you boast, as Paul says, as if you had not received it (1 Corinthians 4:7)? Why do you judge others by displaying yourself? Or does your glory invite others to what is good? But you yourself risk losing it if you boast, and you drive others into the same dangers. What is taken up out of love of glory is easily mocked.

Veil yourself, virgin, if you are a virgin; for you ought to blush. If you are a virgin, do not endure many eyes. Let no one wonder at your face; let no one perceive your lie. You lie well as a married woman if you veil your head. No—you do not seem to lie; for you have married Christ. To him you have handed over your flesh; act according to your husband's teaching. If he commands other men's brides to be veiled, how much more his own.

But do not think the institution of any predecessor should be disturbed. Many surrender their own wisdom and constancy to another's custom. Even if they cannot be compelled to veil, those who are willing should certainly not be forbidden. Those who cannot deny they are virgins—I allow them the misuse of their reputation, with their conscience secure before God. But about those who are said to be betrothed, I can declare and testify beyond my own measure: they must be veiled from the day they first shuddered at the body of a man with a kiss and a handshake. For in them everything has been married beforehand: age through maturity, flesh through years, spirit through consciousness, modesty through the experience of a kiss, hope through expectation, mind through will. And Rebecca is example enough for us: when her betrothed was pointed out, she was veiled for marriage at the mere knowledge of him (Genesis 24:65).
orientation: Tertullian is answering those who say the apostle required only married women to be veiled, by arguing from the word 'woman' itself.

title: When and how to kneel in prayer
english: As for kneeling, prayer also allows some variety in practice because of a few people who refrain from kneeling on the Sabbath. Since this disagreement is currently being argued especially in the churches, the Lord will grant his grace so that they either yield or hold their opinion without causing others to stumble.

But we ourselves, as we have received the tradition, should refrain from kneeling on the day of the Lord's resurrection alone. And not only from kneeling, but from every posture and activity of anxiety. We should also postpone our business affairs, so that we give no place to the devil. The same applies to the whole period of Pentecost, which is marked by the same joyful celebration.

On every other day, who would hesitate to prostrate himself before God, at least in the first prayer with which we enter the daylight? On days of fasting and on fast days, no prayer should be offered without kneeling and the rest of the humble manner. For we do not merely pray, but we entreat and make satisfaction to God our Lord.
About the times of prayer, nothing at all has been prescribed, except plainly to pray at every time and in every place.
orientation: Tertullian is giving practical rules for the bodily posture and times of Christian prayer, after discussing the veiling of virgins.

title: Every place means every place that opportunity or necessity brings
english: But how can we pray in every place, when we are forbidden to pray in public? In every place, he says, that opportunity or even necessity has brought about. For what the apostles did is not reckoned against the precept: they prayed and sang to God in prison while the guards were listening (Acts 16:25). Nor is what Paul did, who performed the eucharist on the ship in the presence of everyone, reckoned against the precept.
orientation: Tertullian is answering an objection to his statement that Christians should pray at every time and in every place, since he also forbids praying in public.

title: Times of Prayer and the Priority of Spiritual Refreshment
english: As for the time of prayer, it will not be useless to observe also certain hours outwardly. I mean the common hours that mark the intervals of the day: the third, the sixth, and the ninth. We find these treated as more solemn in the Scriptures. The Holy Spirit was first poured out upon the gathered disciples at the third hour (Acts 2:1-4). Peter, on the day he experienced the vision of the community of all things in that vessel, had gone up to the upper room at the sixth hour to pray (Acts 10:9). The same Peter, with John, was going up to the temple at the ninth hour, where he restored the paralytic to health (Acts 3:1). These examples stand simply as they are, without any command to observe them. Still, it would be good to establish some settled practice. Such a practice both binds us to the reminder to pray and, as if by a law, sometimes drags us away from our business to this duty. Then, as we read Daniel also observed, certainly from Israelite teaching, we may worship no less than three times a day at least, as debtors of the three: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (Daniel 6:10). This is of course in addition to the regular prayers that are owed without any reminder at the coming of light and of night. It is also fitting for believers not to take food or go to the bath before prayer has been set in between. For the refreshments and nourishments of the spirit must come before those of the flesh, because heavenly things come before earthly things.
orientation: Tertullian is giving practical instruction on the times and customs of Christian prayer, after expounding the Lord's Prayer itself.

title: Greeting a brother with prayer and peace
english: Do not send a brother away without prayer when he has entered your house. “You have seen,” he says, “a brother; you have seen your Lord”—especially if he is a stranger, lest he perhaps be an angel. But neither should you yourself, when received by brothers, put earthly refreshments before heavenly ones. For your faith will be judged immediately. Or how will you say “Peace to this house” according to the command (Matthew 10:12-13), unless you also return mutual peace to those who are in the house?
orientation: Tertullian is giving practical rules for prayer in daily life, now about how to receive a brother who enters your house.

title: Alleluia and Psalms as the Fitting Close of Prayer
english: Those who are more diligent in praying are accustomed to add Alleluia to their prayers, along with psalms of the kind whose closing verses those assembled may answer. And it is certainly an excellent practice, since everything that serves to set God before us and honor Him is fitting, to bring forward a prayer that has been filled full, like a rich sacrificial offering.
orientation: Tertullian is giving practical instructions for the customs of Christian prayer, and here he commends the practice of adding Alleluia and responsive psalms to prayers.

title: The spiritual sacrifice that replaced the old offerings
english: For this is the spiritual sacrifice that has abolished the old sacrifices. “What use to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?” God says. “I am full of burnt offerings of rams, and I do not want the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and goats. For who has required these things from your hands?” (Isaiah 1:11–12). What God has sought instead, the gospel teaches. “The hour is coming,” Jesus says, “when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For God is spirit, and so He requires such worshippers” (John 4:23–24). We are the true worshippers and the true priests, who pray in the Spirit and in the Spirit sacrifice prayer as the victim proper to God and acceptable to Him—the very victim He has required and provided for Himself. This victim, devoted from the whole heart, fed by faith, tended by truth, whole in innocence, clean in chastity, crowned with love, we ought to lead to the altar of God with the procession of good works amid psalms and hymns, and we must obtain everything for ourselves from God.
orientation: Tertullian is concluding his treatise by showing that Christian prayer is the spiritual sacrifice God now requires, replacing the old sacrifices.

title: The power and universal duty of Christian prayer
english: What will God deny to prayer that comes from spirit and truth, when He is the one who demands it? We read and hear and see how many proofs of its power there are! The old prayer used to free people from fires and beasts and hunger, and yet it had not received its form from Christ. How much more, then, does Christian prayer accomplish! It does not station an angel of dew in the middle of the flames, as in the story of Daniel's companions, or shut the mouths of lions, or carry a country meal to the hungry, or turn away any sensation of suffering by a delegated grace. Instead, it trains the patient, those who feel pain, and the grieving in endurance; it enlarges grace by virtue, so that faith may know what it obtains from the Lord, understanding what it suffers for the name of God.

But in former times prayer also used to inflict plagues, scatter enemy armies, and hold back the benefits of rain. Now, however, the prayer of righteousness turns away all the wrath of God, keeps watch for enemies, and begs on behalf of persecutors. Is it any wonder if it knows how to draw down heavenly waters, when it could obtain even fires? Prayer alone is what conquers God; but Christ willed it to work no evil. He conferred on it every power for good.

And so it knows nothing except to call back the souls of the dead from the very road of death, to restore the weak, to heal the sick, to cleanse the demon-possessed, to open prison doors, to loosen the chains of the innocent. It also washes away sins, repels temptations, extinguishes persecutions, comforts the faint-hearted, delights the brave, guides travelers, calms the waves, stuns robbers, feeds the poor, governs the rich, raises the fallen, catches those who are slipping, and holds up those who stand.

Prayer is the wall of faith, our arms and weapons against the enemy who watches us on every side. So let us never walk unarmed. By day let us remember the fast day, by night the vigil. Under the arms of prayer let us guard the standard of our Emperor, and let us wait for the trumpet of the angel while we pray.

All the angels also pray; every creature prays. The cattle and wild beasts pray, and they bend their knees, and as they come out of their stables and caves they look up to heaven with not idle mouth, vibrating their breath in their own way. Even the birds, rising in the morning, lift themselves toward heaven and spread the cross of their wings in place of hands, and say something that seems like prayer. What more, then, is there to say about the duty of prayer? Even the Lord Himself prayed, to whom be honor and power forever and ever.
orientation: Tertullian is concluding the treatise by showing how much more Christian prayer accomplishes than the old prayers, and how all creation prays.
